passage: Sudha was on the crowded local train to college, squeezed against the door, when the message arrived: "Congratulations! Your number has won a new car in our anniversary lucky draw. Pay a small processing tax within 30 minutes to claim." A photo of a shiny red hatchback. Her heart thumped. A car! She pictured driving Mummy to the temple, the look on her cousins' faces. The message said 27 minutes left. The train lurched and the network kept dropping. She started opening her payment app, hands sweaty. Then Avni, her classmate, squashed beside her, glanced at the screen. "Which draw did you enter?" Sudha opened her mouth. She hadn't entered anything. She had never even heard of the shop. The thrill drained out of her so fast she felt dizzy. "If it's real, why would I pay them?" she said slowly. Avni nodded. At the next station Sudha blocked the number and reported the message.

qa.q: What did the message say Sudha had won?
qa.a: A new car in an anniversary lucky draw.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when she first read the message?
qa.a: Sudha felt thrilled and excited, her heart thumping as she pictured driving Mummy to the temple.

qa.q: What question broke the spell, and what did Sudha do next?
qa.a: Avni asked which draw Sudha had entered; seeing she had entered none, Sudha realised the fee was the real theft, then blocked and reported the number.

qa.q: How did Avni help without embarrassing Sudha?
qa.a: Avni asked one simple, curious question instead of mocking, letting Sudha reach the answer herself.

grounding: Shows a person told they have won a car in a draw they never entered and asked for a fee, with the thrill and a countdown cutting thinking short.

subtype: Asking why a stranger would give money [Response]
passage: Vasudha beti, you think these prize tricks started with phones? When I was twenty, working at the post office in Lucknow, a letter came for me on thick yellow paper. It said I had won a foreign lottery, a huge sum, and only had to send a "clearance fee" by money order. In those days that sum was a house. My friend Shafiq said, "Send it quick before they change their mind." But I kept asking myself one thing: what did I enter? I had never bought a foreign ticket in my life. Why would a stranger across the sea give money to Imran of Aminabad? So I took the letter to our postmaster, who wrote to the address it gave. The letter came back: no such company. Shafiq's cousin had sent his fee the month before. He never saw a paisa. A real prize never asks you to pay first, beti. Ask what you entered, and check with someone official.

qa.q: What did the letter ask Imran to send?
qa.a: A clearance fee by money order.

qa.q: What was Imran thinking when Shafiq urged speed?
qa.a: Imran felt doubtful and cautious, puzzled about what he had entered, since he had never bought a foreign ticket.

qa.q: Which choice in the story protected Imran?
qa.a: Taking the letter to the postmaster, who wrote to the address, checked the claim through an official channel before any money was sent.

qa.q: What happened to Shafiq's cousin, and how might he have felt?
qa.a: He sent his fee and never saw a paisa; he likely felt cheated and ashamed.

grounding: Shows a young man asking what he entered, checking the sender through an official channel, and never paying to receive a prize.

passage: It still makes my hands cold to think about it. Last month a call came from someone saying he was from customs: a parcel in my name, with fake passports inside, had been seized in Mumbai. Then a "police officer" in uniform came on video, a station behind him and a badge on the desk. He said I was under "digital arrest", that I must stay on camera, not leave the room and not tell anyone, or my family would be arrested too. For three hours I sat on my bed, nodding, sweating. When he said I could clear my name by transferring my savings to a "verification account", I actually opened my banking app. Then Siddharth, my flatmate, knocked, wanting the charger. I pointed at the phone. He looked at the screen and simply ended the call. I cried and cried. He sat with me, and we called the cybercrime helpline together. Nobody gets arrested over video. I, Swati, had only been frightened into silence.

qa.q: What did the caller say was inside the parcel?
qa.a: Fake passports.

qa.q: How did Swati feel during the three hours on camera?
qa.a: Swati felt terrified and trapped, sweating and nodding, too frightened by the threats to think or ask anyone.

qa.q: What should someone do if a caller claims a digital arrest?
qa.a: End the call, ring the agency's official number themselves, tell family, and report to the cybercrime helpline, as Siddharth and Swati did.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been thinking when he saw the screen?
qa.a: Siddharth likely felt alarmed but clear-headed, seeing threats on a video call, and ended it at once instead of waiting.

grounding: Shows a person kept on a video call by fake officials claiming a parcel is linked to a crime and told to pay, with fear and secrecy stopping them from thinking.

passage:
Supervisor's note, call-centre floor, Tuesday.
At 11:20 Francis's mobile rang at his desk. I saw him go stiff. Afterwards he told me the caller said he was from the "Cyber Crime Branch", that a SIM in his name was linked to a money-laundering case, and that he would be put on a video call and must not disconnect or tell anyone.
Francis did not argue. He said, "I'll call the police station myself," and hung up. His hands were shaking. He looked up the local police station's official number on the government website, not the one the caller gave, and they confirmed they make no arrests over video and ask for no payments. He then phoned his sister, and together we reported it on the cybercrime helpline before lunch.
I've asked Francis to walk the team through it at Friday's meeting. He agreed, looking relieved.
Varun

qa.q: What did the caller say a SIM in Francis's name was linked to?
qa.a: A money-laundering case.

qa.q: How was Francis feeling after he hung up?
qa.a: Francis was frightened, his hands shaking, but steady enough to check; later he looked relieved.

qa.q: Which of Francis's steps made the difference?
qa.a: Hanging up, finding the police station's number himself on the government website, telling his sister, and reporting it to the cybercrime helpline.

qa.q: How might Francis's teammates benefit on Friday?
qa.a: They will hear exactly what such a call sounds like and what to do, so they may feel less frightened and more prepared if it happens to them.

grounding: Shows a person who hangs up on a fake agency, calls the official number himself, tells family and reports to the cybercrime helpline.

subtype: Helping a parent who is targeted [Observer]
passage:
Dear Sarita,
I need to tell you what happened with Papa yesterday, before you hear it from him and worry.
I came home early and found him in his room, door shut, on a video call. A man in a police uniform was telling him to stay silent and not speak to anyone in the house. Papa's face was grey. His chequebook was on the bed and the banking app was already open.
I didn't shout. I sat next to him, took his hand and said, "Papa, I'm here." Then I ended the call. He kept saying sorry, sorry, that they knew his full name and address. I told him, "You did nothing wrong. They do this to thousands of people."
We rang the cybercrime helpline together and reported it. Nothing was sent, thank God.
Please call him tonight, but don't scold him. He's embarrassed enough.
Love,
Payal

qa.q: What did the man in uniform tell Papa to do?
qa.a: To stay silent and not speak to anyone in the house.

qa.q: What does Payal's quiet approach suggest about Payal's feelings?
qa.a: Payal was likely alarmed but chose to stay calm, taking Papa's hand instead of shouting so he would not feel more frightened.

qa.q: Why does Payal ask Sarita not to scold Papa?
qa.a: Because Papa is already embarrassed; blame could make him hide the next call, while kindness keeps him willing to tell them.

qa.q: What was the call like for Papa?
qa.a: Papa was frightened, his face grey and ready to pay, and then ashamed, saying sorry again and again.

grounding: Shows a family member finding an older parent on a long call told to stay silent, staying calm, ending the call, reporting it and not blaming him.

passage:
"Irfan, did you get this?" Vidya held out her phone in the library corridor. "Scholarship refund pending. Click to verify your bank details."
"Yeah, this morning. I nearly clicked. Looked official."
"Look at the sender. It's a random ten-digit number. And the link is misspelled: scholarsip."
"Huh. Okay, that's fake."
"I'm reporting it to the college IT cell. And I'm posting in the class group."
"Everyone will just ignore it."
"Maybe. But Tenzin told me her mother almost paid a refund fee last year. Some people won't spot it."
Irfan went quiet. "My Nani forwards everything. She'd click this in a second."
"Then send it to your family group too. With a screenshot, so she can see what it looks like."
"What do I even say?"
"Keep it simple. Fake message going around. Don't click. If unsure, call me."
Irfan was already typing. "Done. Nani replied with a thumbs-up."

qa.q: How was the link misspelled?
qa.a: It said scholarsip.

qa.q: What seems to motivate Vidya to warn everyone?
qa.a: Vidya feels concerned for people less used to these tricks, like Tenzin's mother, and wants to protect them early.

qa.q: What makes a good warning message, as Vidya suggests?
qa.a: Something short and clear with a screenshot: fake message going around, don't click, if unsure call me.

qa.q: Why might Irfan's Nani be helped by the warning?
qa.a: Nani forwards everything and might click in a second, so a simple screenshot from Irfan helps her recognise the trick and feel safe asking.

grounding: Shows a student who spots a suspicious message, reports it and warns classmates and family, protecting those less used to digital tricks.

passage:
Hi Yusuf,
You asked last week how I always know when a message is fake. I don't! I just slow down. Here's what happened on Monday.
At 7 a.m. I got a text: "Your bank account will be blocked today. Update KYC here," with a link. Then a call from a polite man who said he was from my bank and needed the OTP I'd just received "to stop the block".
I didn't click and I didn't share the OTP. I told him I'd call the bank myself and hung up. Then I checked the sender: a mobile number, not the bank's name. I opened the bank's own app, the one already on my phone, and there was no alert. I called the number printed on my debit card. They said the account was fine, and that no one from the bank would ever ask me for an OTP.
My heart was racing the whole time, by the way. Slowing down doesn't mean feeling calm.
See you Sunday,
Irawati

qa.q: What did the caller ask Irawati for?
qa.a: The OTP just received, to stop the block.

qa.q: How was Irawati feeling while checking?
qa.a: Irawati's heart was racing; Irawati felt anxious even while acting slowly and carefully.

qa.q: Which of Irawati's steps would you advise anyone to copy?
qa.a: Don't click or share the OTP, check the sender, open the bank's own app, and call the number printed on the card.

qa.q: What might Yusuf take from the email?
qa.a: Yusuf may feel reassured that careful people also feel scared, and that a few simple checks matter more than feeling calm.

grounding: Shows a person checking the sender, refusing to click or share an OTP, and contacting the bank directly, which confirms banks never ask for an OTP.

passage: Behind the apartment block in Chennai, Karthik pointed at the water-tank ladder. "Everyone in our gang has touched the top. Unless you're chicken, Pradeep." The others started clucking. Pradeep's face burned. He put one foot on the rusty rung, then another. The ladder wobbled. His stomach flipped. If he came down, they'd laugh all week. If he went up... He came down. "Chicken!" they shouted. At home he couldn't eat his dosa. Amma asked what was wrong, and it all tumbled out. She hugged him. "Coming down was the brave part." Then she called the society secretary, who padlocked the ladder that evening, and she messaged the other parents too.

qa.q: What did Karthik say everyone in the gang had done?
qa.a: Touched the top of the water tank.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel on the ladder?
qa.a: Pradeep felt scared, his stomach flipping, but also afraid of being laughed at all week if he came down.

qa.q: What did Amma do, and why was it important?
qa.a: She praised coming down as brave, then called the society secretary to padlock the ladder and messaged the other parents that same evening, keeping all the children safe.

qa.q: What would change if Pradeep had kept quiet at home?
qa.a: The ladder would still be open and the dare could go on, with Pradeep or another child at risk of a fall.

grounding: Shows a child dared and called chicken to climb an unsafe ladder, torn by fear of exclusion, and an adult's same-day protective step.

subtype: Pressure from friends to prove loyalty [Receiver]
passage: The school bus stopped at the crossing outside their village, and the others were already jumping off. "Come on, Ayesha," Hrithik called. "Everyone's going to the canal. Skip the practice test. Real friends don't ditch the group." Mehwish and Rinku were watching her. The five of them had shared tiffins since Class 5. Ayesha gripped her bag strap. The test mattered; Abbu had taken a day's leave to help her revise. But if she stayed, would they still save her a seat tomorrow? Would the group still be hers? "You're choosing a test over us?" Hrithik said. Her throat went tight. The driver honked. "I'll see you at lunch," she said quietly, and stayed on. The bus pulled away. Through the dusty window she saw Rinku hesitate, then run back and climb in beside her. Neither of them said anything. They didn't need to.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say real friends don't do?
qa.a: Real friends don't ditch the group.

qa.q: What was Ayesha afraid of as she gripped her bag strap?
qa.a: Ayesha felt torn and anxious, afraid that choosing the test would cost her the seat, the tiffins and the whole group.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha hold her ground?
qa.a: A short, calm answer without a fight, then an ally in Rinku, which made the refusal easier to bear.

qa.q: What might Rinku have been feeling when running back to the bus?
qa.a: Rinku probably felt the same pressure and doubt, and Ayesha's quiet no gave Rinku the courage to choose too.

grounding: Shows a teenager told a real friend would skip a test with the group, with the friendship used as leverage and refusal feeling like losing everyone.
